Impulse is the product of the net force and the time for which it acts; it equals the change in momentum.
On Earth, friction and other external forces act on objects, so it is not possible to produce a perfectly force-free situation in which to demonstrate Newton's first law exactly.
Due to inertia, your body tends to remain at rest as the car and seat accelerate forward.
Newton's second law uses the net force because the resultant of all forces determines acceleration; balanced forces have zero resultant.

Use a spring balance to compare the force needed to move a block by sliding it with the force needed to move it on rollers. The smaller force for rolling shows that rolling friction is less than sliding friction.
Terminal velocity is the constant velocity reached when resistive force balances the object's weight, making the resultant force zero.
Fire the rocket away from the spaceship; the reaction pushes the astronaut towards it.
By conservation of momentum, the 80 kg skater moves at 3 m s⁻¹ opposite to the 60 kg skater. They exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
An airbag increases the time over which the passenger's momentum is brought to zero, reducing the rate of change of momentum and therefore the force.
The action and reaction act on different bodies, so they do not cancel on either body. The horse pushes the ground backward, and friction from the ground pushes the horse forward.
Drawing the hands backward increases the time taken to bring the ball's momentum to zero, reducing the force on the hands.
As the jumper pushes off, the boat recoils away from the bank. This can move the support away and cause the jumper to fall short into the water.
Without friction, walking, gripping, writing, and braking would be impossible or very difficult, and objects would slide without friction to oppose their motion.
Force is a push or pull that can change an object's state of rest or motion, direction, or shape. Examples include kicking a ball and pushing a cart.

The first law describes inertia: an object remains at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force. The second law relates net force to the rate of change of momentum. The third law states that action and reaction forces are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.
Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, p = mv. Newton's second law states that net force equals the rate of change of momentum: F = Δp/Δt.
If no external resultant force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant; total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum afterwards.
Static friction opposes the start of sliding and increases up to a limiting value. Once the block slides, kinetic friction acts opposite to the relative motion of the surfaces.
Friction between tyres and the road provides grip for starting, turning, and braking. Tread helps maintain grip, while braking friction opposes motion and slows or stops the vehicle.
